framework: Assessment reform for the age of artificial intelligence
issuer: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (TEQSA); authors Lodge J.M., Howard S., Bearman M., Dawson P. and associates
year_or_version: November 2023 (discussion paper Sept 2023; final launched 23 Nov 2023)
relevant_provisions: Guiding principle 1: assessment should prepare students to take part ethically and actively in a society where AI is everywhere. Guiding principle 2: trustworthy judgements need multiple, inclusive and contextualised assessments, not one assessment type. Propositions: assessment should emphasise (1) appropriate authentic engagement with AI; (2) a programmatic approach; (3) the process of learning; (4) working appropriately with others and AI; (5) security at meaningful points across a program. Preamble names fairness, accessibility, transparency, equity and a right to privacy as foundations and aligns with HESF 1.4, 5.2 and 2.2.
applicability_notes: Commissioned advice, not a TEQSA Guidance Note and explicitly not prescriptive. Strong support for the project's process-evidence and viva design (propositions 3 and 5). Its own privacy principle is a check on capturing keystrokes. Note: the PDF linked from the official page still has 'discussion-paper' in its file name but its cover reads November 2023.

framework: Gen AI strategies for Australian higher education: Emerging practice (toolkit)
issuer: TEQSA
year_or_version: 28 November 2024
relevant_provisions: Built from providers' responses to TEQSA's June 2024 request for information on credible action plans for gen AI risk to award integrity (100% response). Three dimensions: Process, People, Practice. Warns that AI-detection tools carry false-positive and bias risks and are not enough for assessment security alone. Says guidelines should not compromise students' safety, privacy or intellectual property. Gives a 'two-lane' example and lists interactive oral assessments and vivas as secure options. Includes a provider case where students can submit AI chat logs with assessments, handled under privacy law.
applicability_notes: Emerging-practice examples, not mandatory. Directly relevant: precedent for submitting AI-use logs and for vivas. Companion: Gen AI strategies for research training (June 2025).

framework: Enacting assessment reform in a time of artificial intelligence
issuer: TEQSA
year_or_version: 24 September 2025 (page date; PDF hosted in a 2026-06 folder)
relevant_provisions: Follow-up to the 2023 paper with implementation pathways: program-wide reform, unit-level assurance (at least one secure task per unit, with a check that the person is the enrolled student) and a hybrid. Says institutions should focus on redesigning assessment rather than investing mainly in detection. Warns that falling back on invigilated exams can reduce authenticity and make inequity worse.
applicability_notes: Later TEQSA guidance, not prescriptive. Useful for justifying vivas as the 'secure' point in a hybrid model.

framework: Higher Education Standards Framework (Threshold Standards) 2021
issuer: Commonwealth Minister for Education, made under s58(1) TEQSA Act 2011; Federal Register of Legislation F2021L00488
year_or_version: Current compilation C02 (F2026C00804) from 14 July 2026, incorporating the HESF Amendment (Threshold Standards) Instrument 2026 (F2026L00954). Previous compilation C01 F2022C00105.
relevant_provisions: 1.4.3: assessment methods match the learning outcomes, can confirm all outcomes are achieved, and grades reflect attainment. 5.2.1-5.2.3: policies uphold academic integrity; preventative action against cheating and misrepresentation; students get guidance on misconduct and good practice. 2.2.1: practices accommodate student diversity and give equivalent opportunities for success. 2.3: wellbeing and safety on campus and online (2.3.3 support informed by disability and mental health needs). 7.3.3(b): information systems are kept securely and confidentially to prevent unauthorised access to private or sensitive information.
applicability_notes: Binding on Adelaide University as a registered provider. SURPRISE: the 2026 amendment (made 9 July 2026, registered 13 July 2026) replaces 2.3(4) ('safe and inclusive environment ... on campus and online'), inserts 6.4 (preventing and responding to racism) and 6.10 (consultation with students and staff). Schedule 1 changes apply from 1 January 2027 and the old text continues until then. Standards 1.4, 5.2 and 7.3 are unchanged.

framework: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) and Australian Privacy Principles (APPs): coverage of state universities
issuer: Commonwealth Parliament; regulator Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC)
year_or_version: Privacy Act 1988 as amended; statutory tort in Schedule 2 commenced 10 June 2025
relevant_provisions: OAIC states the Act does not cover state or territory government agencies, or a university other than a private university and the ANU. APPs still apply where a university handles personal information for Commonwealth-funded activities. Schedule 2 statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy (intrusion upon seclusion or misuse of information; intentional or reckless; serious) has applied to conduct since 10 June 2025.
applicability_notes: Adelaide University is a public university under the Adelaide University Act 2023 (SA), so the APPs do not bind all of its activities. Its Privacy Policy (effective 1 Jan 2026) says it is not subject to the APPs for all activities, must comply for Commonwealth-funded operations, and has adopted APP-consistent practices across all operations. Uncertain: whether the statutory tort could reach a university's student monitoring. It is not limited to APP entities, but there are defences such as consent and lawful authority. Pending: Privacy Amendment (Personal Data Protection) Bill 2026 exposure draft (Aug 2026), not yet law.

framework: Information Privacy Principles (IPPs) Instruction (PC012; Cabinet Administrative Instruction 1/89)
issuer: Government of South Australia, Department of the Premier and Cabinet; administered via State Records / Privacy Committee of SA
year_or_version: Effective from May 2020 (last amended 4 May 2020; commencement clause 1 July 2016)
relevant_provisions: Cl 2(2): applies to 'public sector agencies' as defined in s3(1) of the Public Sector Act 2009 (SA). IPP 1: do not collect personal information unlawfully, unfairly or unnecessarily. IPP 2: tell the person the purpose of collection. IPP 3: do not collect information that is irrelevant or excessively personal. IPP 4: store it securely. Later IPPs limit use and disclosure to the collection purpose unless an exception applies.
applicability_notes: UNCERTAIN APPLICABILITY: SA has no general privacy statute; the IPPI is an administrative instruction, not legislation. Whether a university is a 'public sector agency' under the Public Sector Act 2009 was not confirmed, and universities are not in the exclusion schedule. Adelaide University's Privacy Policy lists the IPPI as related legislation without saying it is binding. Safest framing: Adelaide University voluntarily follows APP-consistent practice, and the IPPI's collection-minimisation principles are a relevant benchmark. No SA privacy bill was found.

framework: Adelaide University Privacy Policy
issuer: Adelaide University
year_or_version: Effective 1 January 2026 (approved 1 May 2024; updated 19 Dec 2025)
relevant_provisions: Says the University is not subject to the APPs for all activities but complies for Commonwealth-funded operations and follows APP-consistent practice across all operations. Applies GDPR to individuals in the EU. Discloses that personal information is collected by monitoring and logging metadata from use of University IT services, and lists 'monitoring your progress in your course of study' as a purpose.
applicability_notes: The governing institutional instrument for any AI-log capture. Keystroke or prompt capture would go beyond 'metadata' logging, so a specific collection notice and purpose statement would be needed.

framework: Copyright Act 1968 (Cth)
issuer: Commonwealth Parliament; administered by Attorney-General's Department
year_or_version: Compilation C65 (C2026C00138) from 2 April 2026, incorporating the Copyright Amendment Act 2026 (Act No. 29 of 2026)
relevant_provisions: s40(1): fair dealing with a work for research or study is not an infringement. s40(2): fairness factors are purpose, nature of the work, commercial availability, market effect and amount taken. s40(3): copying an article from a periodical for research or study is deemed fair. s41: fair dealing for criticism or review needs sufficient acknowledgement. Moral rights (Part IX, s193 attribution; s195AO infringement) require correct attribution of authors.
applicability_notes: Quoting and summarising papers in a student report fits ss40-41 if acknowledged. Australia has no general fair use and no text and data mining exception; per secondary sources, the 2026 amendment covers orphan works and the s28 education exception and adds no TDM exception (2026 amendment contents not read in the statute itself). Facts in datasets are not themselves protected, but the compilation or database may be, so follow the licence.

framework: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) legal code
issuer: Creative Commons
year_or_version: Version 4.0 (2013)
relevant_provisions: s2(a)(1)(A): you may reproduce and Share the material, in whole or in part, for NonCommercial purposes only. s2(a)(1)(B): you may produce and reproduce Adapted Material but may not Share it. s3(a): attribution, licence notice, link and an indication of any changes are required when Sharing. s4: database rights allow extracting and reusing contents NonCommercially, provided Adapted Material is not Shared. s2(a)(2): exceptions such as fair dealing are not limited by the licence.
applicability_notes: KEY POINT: you may compute statistics and analyses from an ND dataset privately, but publishing a modified or derived version of the dataset (filtered, recoded, merged) is not permitted. Reporting your own findings (counts, charts, conclusions) is generally treated as new work rather than Adapted Material, but this is a judgement call. Do not redistribute cleaned ND data files. The CC BY 4.0 datasets allow adaptation and sharing with attribution.

framework: Australia's AI Ethics Principles
issuer: Department of Industry, Science and Resources (DISR), Australian Government
year_or_version: Published 7 November 2019; page updated 2 December 2025
relevant_provisions: 8 voluntary principles. Relevant: Privacy protection and security (uphold privacy rights and data protection; secure data). Fairness (inclusive, accessible, no unfair discrimination). Transparency and explainability (people should know when AI significantly affects them). Contestability (a timely way to challenge AI use or outcomes). Accountability and human oversight.
applicability_notes: Voluntary, not law. SURPRISE: DISR now describes the principles in the past tense. Its Guidance for AI Adoption (21 Oct 2025, 6 essential practices) is presented as the updated, simplified successor that builds on these principles and the Voluntary AI Safety Standard. Cite both. Relevant to any AI-assisted review of the captured logs: students must be able to contest outcomes.

framework: ACS Code of Professional Ethics
issuer: Australian Computer Society (ACS)
year_or_version: 2023; adopted into ACS National Regulations (NR4) on 14 March 2023
relevant_provisions: Values: honesty, trustworthiness, respect. 2.1(a)-(b): be honest and do not misrepresent your capability, which links to AI-use disclosure. 2.2(d): respect the privacy, confidentiality and integrity of personal information, including data about individuals. 2.2(h): build robust, secure systems. 2.3.1(c),(f),(g): do not discriminate unfairly in system design, reduce risks to others, and respect others' intellectual property.
applicability_notes: Binds ACS members; a professional benchmark for computing graduates and for designing the capture system. Still listed as current on the ACS ethics page (Oct 2026). The older Code of Professional Conduct v2.1 is still hosted alongside it.

framework: National Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research
issuer: NHMRC, with ARC and Universities Australia
year_or_version: SURPRISE: the 2023 edition was RESCINDED. The 2025 edition has been in effect since 23 June 2026; the 2023 edition applied 1 Jan 2024 to 22 June 2026.
relevant_provisions: 5.1.15: an institution may exempt lower-risk research meeting 5.1.17 from ethics review. 5.1.16: research using personal information without consent cannot be exempted. 5.1.17(a): exemption may cover research using data with all identifiers removed before the researchers received it, if they agree not to re-identify, to prevent unauthorised access, and that sharing will not add re-identification risk. 5.1.17(c): educational training activities whose outputs are for program use only. 5.1.18: exemption decisions must be recorded. The old 'negligible risk' tier was replaced by 'lower risk' in the 2023 update.
applicability_notes: Cite the 2025 edition, not 2023. Secondary analysis of public de-identified datasets likely fits 5.1.17(a) and/or (c), but the institution grants the exemption, not the researchers. Adelaide University Human Research Ethics Procedure (effective 18 Dec 2025) s3.4-3.5 requires approval or exemption before research starts and copies the 5.1.17 criteria. Any future pilot of the log-capture system with real students would need full ethics review.

framework: Australian Code for the Responsible Conduct of Research, 2018
issuer: NHMRC, Australian Research Council and Universities Australia
year_or_version: 2018 (marked Current on NHMRC site, Oct 2026)
relevant_provisions: Principles P1 honesty, P2 rigour, P3 transparency in reporting methods, data and findings, P6 recognition of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples' right to be engaged. R21: use methods suited to the aims and draw conclusions justified by results. R22: keep clear, accurate, secure and complete records of research data. R23: disseminate findings accurately. R27: cite and acknowledge other work appropriately.
applicability_notes: Applies through Adelaide University's Research Integrity Policy. Supports transparent disclosure of the dual-AI screening and adjudication method (P3, R21) and correct citation (R27). Supported by the guide 'Management of Data and Information in Research'.

framework: Disability Standards for Education 2005 (Cth)
issuer: Commonwealth Attorney-General, made under the Disability Discrimination Act 1992; Register F2005L00767
year_or_version: SURPRISE: amended by the Disability Standards for Education Amendment Standards 2025 (F2025L01390); current compilation C01 (F2026C00801) from 1 August 2026
relevant_provisions: 3.4(1)-(2): an adjustment is reasonable if it balances the interests of all affected parties, considering the student's disability, their views, and effects on learning outcomes, participation and independence. 3.4(3): the provider may keep the academic requirements inherent to the course; the note lets it protect assessment integrity. 3.5: the provider must consult the student before adjusting, including on less intrusive alternatives. 6.3(a),(f): assessment requirements must suit the student's needs and be accessible; assessment methods must be adapted so the student can demonstrate the skills assessed. New 6.1A states a right to participate on the same basis as other students.
applicability_notes: Directly relevant to vivas (e.g. anxiety, speech, hearing or neurodivergence needs), to keystroke capture (assistive technology such as dictation or screen readers produces atypical logs), and to time limits. Provisions cited are from the 2026 compilation; verify numbering if citing the 2005 as-made text.

framework: Guidance for generative AI in education and research
issuer: UNESCO; authors Fengchun Miao and Wayne Holmes
year_or_version: 2023 (published 7 September 2023); UNESDOC ark:/48223/pf0000386693; web page last updated 16 Jan 2026
relevant_provisions: Proposes regulatory steps with a human-centred approach, including requiring data privacy protection and setting an age limit for independent use of GenAI platforms. Calls for ethical validation of GenAI tools and pedagogical designs that protect human agency. Urges institutions to build coherent policy frameworks.
applicability_notes: International soft guidance, not binding. Supports human agency (keeping humans as decision-makers, e.g. in vivas) and data protection for student AI logs. The age-13 figure often quoted was NOT shown on the landing page; check the full PDF before citing it.

framework: Adelaide University Academic Integrity Policy
issuer: Adelaide University (approved by Vice Chancellor and President)
year_or_version: Effective 28 May 2024; revised 1 January 2025
relevant_provisions: Four academic integrity principles, e.g. (2) alleged misconduct handled fairly and transparently without bias. Defines 'Inappropriate use of artificial intelligence (AI)' as misconduct: submitting work wholly or partly produced by generative AI as one's own; using AI-generated information without acknowledgement; using AI or digital tools to misrepresent competence or hide other misconduct.
applicability_notes: Applies to the whole Adelaide University community. No formal clause numbers. The page notes some role titles are still placeholders.

framework: Adelaide University Academic Misconduct Procedure; Assessment Procedure
issuer: Adelaide University
year_or_version: Misconduct Procedure effective 14 January 2025; Assessment Procedure effective 17 February 2025
relevant_provisions: Misconduct Procedure s1: software is used to help prevent and detect misconduct. s7: academic misconduct meeting, usually online. Findings are on the balance of probabilities. s13: outcomes table for inappropriate AI use, standard outcome up to zero for the task. Assessment Procedure s2: Course Coordinators design and secure tasks to prevent and detect misconduct. s6: students must be told about appropriate use of generative AI. s8: 'certified assessment' (examples include interviews) requires identity checks and invigilation.
applicability_notes: No public AI-use levels framework, AI-use statement template or viva-for-verification rule was found. The project's proposal would extend s6 and s8. IT Acceptable Use Policy (effective 19 Dec 2025; s3.6 amended 29 Sept 2026) states continuous monitoring of IT use and that users consent to it by using the systems. It does not mention AI. Legacy University of Adelaide 'Working with AI' student page now redirects to the Academic Integrity Policy.

framework: CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance
issuer: Global Indigenous Data Alliance (GIDA)
year_or_version: Drafted Nov 2018 (Gaborone workshop); released Sept 2019
relevant_provisions: Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility, Ethics: people- and purpose-centred principles that complement FAIR. They cover Indigenous rights to govern data about their peoples, lands and knowledges.
applicability_notes: LIMITED RELEVANCE: the project's datasets are not Indigenous data and no Indigenous communities are studied. The GIDA page itself did not list the sub-elements; the four names were confirmed through secondary university sources. Mention briefly: any future log-capture system would collect data on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students, so governance should consider collective interests. HESF 2.2.2 and Code P6/R19 also apply.

framework: Maiam nayri Wingara Indigenous Data Sovereignty Principles
issuer: Maiam nayri Wingara Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Data Sovereignty Collective (with Australian Indigenous Governance Institute)
year_or_version: 2018 (Indigenous Data Sovereignty Summit Communique)
relevant_provisions: Rights of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples to: exercise control of the data ecosystem; data that is contextual and disaggregated; data that is relevant and supports self-determination; data structures accountable to Indigenous peoples; data that is protective of individual and collective interests.
applicability_notes: LIMITED RELEVANCE for the secondary-analysis methods. Becomes relevant if student AI-use data is disaggregated by Indigenous status or used in equity monitoring. Adelaide University's Human Research Ethics Procedure s3.1 also requires the NHMRC 2018 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander research guidelines and the AIATSIS Code (2020) for research involving these peoples.

framework: Surveillance Devices Act 2016 (SA)
issuer: Parliament of South Australia; legislation.sa.gov.au
year_or_version: Version 21.9.2023 (current consolidated); in operation since 18 Dec 2017
relevant_provisions: s3: a 'data surveillance device' is a program or device that can access, track, monitor or record information going into or out of a computer, which covers keystroke and prompt loggers. s8(1): it is an offence to knowingly install, use or maintain one without the express or implied consent of the computer's owner or the person lawfully controlling it (maximum penalty $75,000 for a body corporate). s8(2): exceptions where authorised by law or in prescribed circumstances.
applicability_notes: APPLIES TO STUDENTS, not just workers: consent is tied to the computer's owner or controller, not employment. Logging inside a University-owned or controlled workspace is likely covered by University consent. Capturing keystrokes on a student-owned device would need the student's express consent. SA has no workplace-surveillance statute like NSW's, and OAIC has no specific student-monitoring guidance (none found). Privacy Act employee-records exemption is irrelevant to students. University staff WHS 'Workplace Monitoring Protocol' is about hazards, not IT surveillance. See also HESF 7.3.3(b), University IT Acceptable Use Policy s3.6 and Privacy Policy.
